Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• The concept of student growth isn’t as difficult to understand and popular
 perception suggests.
• Calculations may be complicated but knowing how to calculate student
 growth is not synonymous with understanding student growth:
 – The number π (pi=3.14159…) is difficult to calculate but is simple to
 understand conceptually.
 – Height and weight percentiles associated with children are difficult to
 calculate but are simple to understand conceptually.
• Computational details are important but often obscure a simple conceptual
 basis.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• There are 3 general approaches of
 calculating student growth:
 – Growth as an amount of change (i.e., gain).
 – Growth as a norm/peer referenced quantity.
 – Growth as a criterion referenced quantity.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• Growth as an amount of change:
 – What could be more simple?

 – Requires a vertical scale (which Arizona now has)

• Not as simple as it seems:
 – Comparisons between students often leads to wrong conclusions
 – Interpreting change requires context.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts
• This is analogous to height/weight measures for infants.
• Growth amounts are tricky to interpret and require context.
• Peer based comparisons used by growth analyses are a way to acquire that context.

 An infant male toddler is measured at 2 and 3 years of age
 and is shown to have grown 4 inches. The magnitude of
 increase—4 inches—is a well understood quantity that any
 parent can grasp and calculate at home using a simple
 yardstick. However, parents leaving their pediatrician’s office
 knowing only how much their child has grown would likely be
 wanting for more information: Parents are not interested in
 an absolute magnitude of growth, but instead in a norm-
 referenced quantity locating that 4 inch increase alongside
 the height increases of similar children.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts

• Peer-based analyses are also called norm-referenced analyses.
• Like with infant height/weight charts, peers are children/student
 with similar characteristics.
• For growth analyses using large scale assessments, peers are
 students with (at least) the same scale score history on the same
 tests.
• Peer based norms are invaluable in providing context for
 stakeholders to understand student growth.
• The Arizona SGP Model (i.e., the Colorado Growth Model) creates
 growth norms for all students using regression (i.e., peer-based)
 analyses.
• These norms allow stakeholders to understand what an ambitious yet
 reasonable expectation is for each student.

Growth Model: Other Options
• Almost all current growth model use large amounts of
 data to create “norms” against which student growth is
 judged.
• Absent large amounts of data (>1,000 grade/content
 area), professional judgment (usually based upon a
 “norm”) replaces large-scale data-based norms.
• Value-tables can be used to monitor progress of
 students between achievement bands established for
 year-to-year assessments.
• Some states (e.g., Alaska) use value-tables, particularly
 with smaller scale assessments for evaluating student
 growth for accountability purposes.

 Student Growth Percentiles: Concepts and Calculation 18

Student Growth Percentiles

• Research on the SGP model began in 2007.
• Based upon work in Colorado, the norm-referenced model
 was extended to include a criterion-referenced
 component.
• Work in other states incorporating the model into state
 reporting and accountability systems occurred in
 subsequent years and student growth became more
 common across state assessment systems.
• Goal or the model is to create an individual level growth
 metric that is informative to different stakeholders ranging
 from parents to policy makers.

What is R?

• Interpreted programming language tailored for statistics.
 – Instructions/commands are entered at a prompt, interpreted and
 executed before moving on to the next
 – In contrast to C, C++, FORTRAN, etc. that are compiled before execution.
 Note: Some R functions use these languages in the background to
 provide more efficiency.
 – A set of instructions can be combined into an R script (usually with
 the .R extension) and “sourced” to run the entire set of commands at
 once.
• Graphical engine.
 – Produce plots and reports such as those shown here.
• Data manipulation and management to a lesser extent.

 Student Growth Percentiles: Concepts and Calculation 21

What is R?

• Object oriented language. Everything is an object.
 – Single characters or numbers.
 – Functions (which are often composed of other, more ‘primitive’
 functions – R is mostly written in R).
 – Data
 • Data structures include vectors, matrices, arrays, data frames (an important
 variation of this is the data.table)
 • User can have multiple datasets open at one time unlike other stats
 software.
 – Results (model summaries, predictions, residuals). Probably the most
 important. In the end we want some product (statistics, graphics, etc.).

 Student Growth Percentiles: Concepts and Calculation 22

R Packages

• R is highly extensible through the creation of R packages.
• A “package” is a collection of functions, documentation, data and
 other things that are often tailored for a particular purpose. A user
 loads a package into R in order to use these functions. A collection
 of packages makes a “library”.
• R has a BASE package of statistical and graphical functions upon
 which many more can be added.
• Many R packages depend on other packages in order to work. That
 is, many R functions are built upon other R functions. This is one of
 the main advantages of open source R. You are free to build on,
 change or borrow other peoples work in order to create your own
 software.

SGP Package

• First version available on CRAN in October, 2008.
• Now uses functions from 30 other R packages.
 – Functions from these packages (and data) are imported and used in SGP’s
 functions.
 – Most essential dependency is rq function from quantreg – the quantile
 regression package developed by R. Koenker.
• Stable version is available on CRAN:
 http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/SGP/index.html
• Development version (and visible code) is available on GitHub:
 – www.SGP.io
 – https://github.com/CenterForAssessment/SGP

 Student Growth Percentiles: Concepts and Calculation 24

SGP Package

• 84 functions in the package (27 exported).
 – Two key functions are studentGrowthPercentiles and
 studentGrowthProjections.
 – “Wrapper” functions for analyzing data. Higher level functions that do a
 lot of data management and bookkeeping, but are largely built around
 the two key lower level functions and their output.
 – Utility and convenience functions that perform tasks that are often
 repeated. These help with the bookkeeping mentioned above, and are
 largely only used internally (they are not “exported” functions).
 – Visualization and data export functions.
 – meta-data for state level assessment programs is embedded in a data
 object inside the SGP package: SGPstateData.

Installation

• To install from CRAN simply start R and type:
install.packages(“SGP”)
• To install from Github you need:
 – Windows: Rtools (http://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/),
 – OS X: xcode (from the app store)
 – Linux: apt-get install r-base-dev (or similar)
install.packages("devtools")
require(devtools)
install_github(”centerforassessment/SGP")
require(SGP)

• Installation instructions are also available HERE.
